hints: Look closely at Fig. 8.1 - the dark structures are thick, short and clearly visible as separate bodies. What must have happened to the long, thin chromatin present in interphase to make them look like this?
Notice that many of the structures look like pairs stuck closely together side-by-side, not single isolated threads. What special pairing unique to meiosis I brings matching chromosomes together?
Think about what happens when those paired chromatids break and swap sections with each other. Which chromatids are involved, and what is this exchange called?
In late prophase I the paired chromosomes start to pull slightly apart but stay attached at certain points. What is the name for these attachment points where exchange occurred?
walkthrough:
Why Chromosomes Become Visible**
You can actually see dark, thick bodies in the photo because the DNA has coiled up very tightly. In interphase the chromatin is long and spread out, so it stains faintly. During prophase I it supercoils and condenses, becoming shorter and thicker, which is why each chromosome shows up as a dark stained structure.

Pairing Up Into Bivalents**
This is meiosis, not mitosis, so something special happens. Each chromosome has already replicated into two sister chromatids, and now the two homologous chromosomes - one maternal and one paternal with the same genes in the same loci - come together side-by-side. This close pairing is called synapsis and the pair is called a bivalent or tetrad because it contains four chromatids.

Crossing Over Between Non-Sister Chromatids**
While paired, non-sister chromatids - that means one chromatid from one homologue and one chromatid from the other homologue - break at the same locus and swap sections. This is crossing over. It involves breaking and rejoining of DNA, so alleles are exchanged and new combinations are created.

Chiasmata Hold Them Together**
By late prophase I, as in Fig. 8.1, the homologues try to separate slightly but stay joined where crossing over happened. Those X-shaped join points are called chiasmata. That is why you see looped, crossed and joined shapes rather than neat single rods.

Final answer: Chromatin / chromosomes condense and become visible. Homologous chromosomes pair up by synapsis to form bivalents / tetrads. Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids with exchange of sections. Homologues remain joined at chiasmata / crossover points.
